findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Dockerfile:3 downloads mutable remote content and pipes it directly to sh during every image build, allowing a compromised or changed endpoint to execute arbitrary code in the image build environment.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: The added build step downloads mutable remote content and immediately executes it. A compromise or change at that URL can alter the produced image without a repository change or integrity verification.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This newly added build step fetches and executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh serves at build time. A compromised or changed endpoint can inject arbitrary commands into the image and makes builds non-reproducible.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in the exported wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported wrapper discards that signal and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish an absent key from a present key whose value is legitimately empty.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key status in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this public function discards it and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a present key whose legitimate stored value is empty.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failure in the public wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this wrapper discards it and returns "", which is also a valid stored value. Public callers cannot distinguish failure from a successful empty-string load.

findings.title: Wait for dispatched result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed goroutines can still send on results after Run returns. A caller that closes results after Run completes can trigger a "send on closed channel" panic, and callers can observe completion before all results are delivered.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every `results <- j * 2` completed. It now returns immediately after launching goroutines. A caller that treats return as completion—for example, by closing `results` after Run returns—can cause the launched goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel"; callers also cannot reliably consume all results before observing completion.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: The new goroutines detach each result send from Run. Callers can close the results channel or assume all results are available immediately after Run returns, causing a send-on-closed-channel panic or incomplete results.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `||` predicate returns true for an admin from tenant A deleting a record in tenant B. This removes tenant isolation from the exported destructive-action authorization check.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant ownership
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `||` returns true for same-tenant non-admins and for admins from other tenants, bypassing the prior tenant-scoped administrative deletion requirement.

findings.title: Require admin status before deleting a record
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || makes canDeleteRecord return true for any session whose tenant matches the record, even when session.isAdmin is false. This removes the prior admin requirement from a public deletion authorization decision.

findings.title: Preserve invalid-settings errors before saving
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch converts JSON parsing and schema-validation errors into defaults. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and saves it, overwriting the supplied stored value rather than propagating the invalid-settings error.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of defaulting and saving over settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch converts malformed or schema-invalid stored settings into defaults. updateFontSize then changes the font size and saves that fallback, overwriting the original settings instead of preserving the previously observable parse failure.

findings.title: Preserve parse errors before saving settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed catch at src/settings.ts:14-15 converts malformed or schema-invalid settings into defaults. updateFontSize then changes the font size and saves the fallback document at src/settings.ts:20-22, silently replacing the invalid stored value instead of reporting the parse failure.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return uses build.ref("verified") for artifacts while builtFrom remains build.ref(branch). If the refs differ, callers receive artifacts for a different commit than the one the report identifies.

findings.title: Use the selected branch commit for report artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` is resolved from `branch`, while `artifacts` are now fetched from `verified`. If those refs differ, the returned report associates artifacts from one commit with another commit.

findings.title: Use the reported commit when loading artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport sets builtFrom from build.ref(branch) but loads artifacts from build.ref("verified"). If those refs differ, the report associates artifacts from the verified commit with the requested branch's commit.

findings.title: Restore the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit. The renderFeed caller passes 20 and iterates the entire returned page, extending its 20-element array for feeds with more than 20 entries.

findings.title: Restore the limit bound in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit smaller than all.length, this returns every entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed calls it with 20 at src/feed.ts:9; with 21 inputs, its loop writes index 20 and extends the intended 20-slot output to 21 entries.

findings.title: Restore the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all entries rather than at most limit. renderFeed calls recentEntries(all, 20), so feeds with over 20 entries now return more than 20 items.

findings.title: Count only rows emitted into the manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: When an entry is stale, its row is removed but `# entry-count` still uses `entries.length`. The serialized manifest therefore advertises more entries than it contains, breaking consumers that validate or preallocate from the header.

findings.title: Count only rendered entries in the manifest header
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is omitted but `# entry-count` still uses `entries.length`. Two entries with one stale therefore produce one data row and `# entry-count: 2`, making the exported manifest internally inconsistent.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The new filter removes stale entries from the emitted rows, but the header still uses `entries.length`. One live and one stale entry therefore declares `# entry-count: 2` while emitting only one row.

findings.title: Retain the exported legacy formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: This deletes the public ids.FormatLegacyID symbol. Any downstream package that previously used it will fail to compile after upgrading, with undefined: ids.FormatLegacyID.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was exported before this change, but src/orders.ts now exports only Order and orderTotal. Existing consumers importing shippingQuote from this module will fail to compile or load after upgrade.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed module no longer exports shippingQuote; existing TypeScript imports fail to compile and JavaScript consumers receive no such named export.

findings.title: Reject non-string stored hashes instead of raising
findings.whyItBreaks: `hmac.compare_digest` raises `TypeError` when its string hash is compared with `None` or bytes. The prior equality check returned `False`, allowing `guard()` to return its 401 denial response; this changed line instead exits before that branch.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute(input) is publicly typed to return a string, but every invocation now throws "always fails". The previous implementation returned the uppercase input, so this is a complete regression for all consumers.

findings.title: Return the execution result instead of always throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute(input): string API now throws "always fails", so callers cannot obtain the string result that this function returned before the change.

findings.title: Restore execute's declared string-returning behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed implementation unconditionally throws, so callers of the exported execute(input): string API receive an exception for every input rather than the promised string result.

findings.title: Keep viewer requests on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 and can no longer return its explicit "read-only" result at line 25.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now fails `isEligible` at `src/handler.ts:18`, causing `handle` to return "rejected" at `src/handler.ts:24`; its subsequent "read-only" branch at `src/handler.ts:25` is unreachable.

findings.title: Keep active viewers on the read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: The new viewer exclusion causes active viewers below the attempt limit to return "rejected" before handle reaches its dedicated "read-only" branch.

findings.title: Keep unpaid drafts saveable
findings.whyItBreaks: For `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`, the new payment predicate returns false. `saveDraft` consumes this shared result at src/actions.ts:9 and returns "blocked", whereas this order was previously saved. Payment is a legitimate prerequisite for submitting an order, but not for saving its draft state.

findings.title: Keep the payment gate out of draft saving
findings.whyItBreaks: For an order with state="draft" and payment="missing", the new predicate returns false. saveDraft uses this shared predicate at src/actions.ts:9, so it now returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Payment legitimately governs submitting an order, but not persisting an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Keep payment gating out of draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed predicate rejects `{ state: "draft", payment: "missing" }`. `saveDraft` calls this predicate and returns "blocked", so unpaid drafts can no longer be saved.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When channel is not "stable", the returned Snapshot.commit identifies that channel's head but Snapshot.files comes from stable. Consumers publishing or inspecting the snapshot will associate the wrong file set with the recorded commit.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The returned snapshot reports the requested channel's head as `commit`, but reads `files` from the `stable` head. For any channel other than `stable`, the snapshot's commit and files describe different revisions.

findings.title: Read files from the published channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return value sets `Snapshot.commit` to the requested channel head, but reads `Snapshot.files` from `stable`. When those refs differ, consumers receive an inconsistent snapshot.

findings.title: Honor the limit argument
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still iterates over the hard-coded `max_count = 10`, returning ten items. The public parameter promises a caller-observable limit but has no effect.

findings.title: Honor the public limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns ten items because the changed signature exposes a caller-specified cap while the body always iterates the hard-coded `max_count = 10`.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build("x", limit=3)` still returns 10 items because the newly added `limit` argument is never used; the function always iterates `range(max_count)` where `max_count` is 10.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly named parse_positive_int still returns 0 and negative integers. charge() consumes that result directly, producing zero or negative cents rather than rejecting an invalid amount.

findings.title: Enforce positivity before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed parse_positive_int promises a positive integer but returns int(value) unchanged. "0" and "-1" therefore reach charge and produce 0 and -100 cents instead of being rejected.

findings.title: Validate positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1, so charge('-1') returns -100 despite the public function's positive-integer contract. A caller using this parser to validate charge amounts can therefore create a negative charge.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function wrote to a copy and returned it, leaving df unchanged. It now writes directly into df, so callers that retain or reuse the input silently observe their original data modified.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed assignments now target df directly. The base revision copied df and returned the modified copy, so callers that retain df will now observe it being modified after apply_values returns.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame when applying values
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation copied df before updating rows, so callers could retain and reuse their original DataFrame. This change writes directly through df.loc and returns the same object, causing later use of the caller's DataFrame to observe transformed values.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1` and `parse_positive_int("0")` returns `0`, despite its public name promising a positive result. The changed internal caller consequently makes `charge("-1")` return `-100`, so consumers cannot safely rely on the newly advertised contract.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1` and `parse_positive_int("0")` returns `0`, contradicting the newly introduced public positive-integer promise. Its direct consumer then produces negative or zero charges.

findings.title: Reject non-positive parsed values
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1` and `parse_positive_int("0")` returns `0`, contradicting its new public positive-value contract. Its direct consumer, `charge` at `src/parse.rs:6`, therefore returns `-100` for `"-1"`.

findings.title: Remove the debug expression that consumes `items`
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and returns the `Vec<String>` by value; because its result is discarded, `items` is moved before the following `items.len()` call. Rust rejects this with a use-after-move compilation error, blocking all consumers of `process`.

findings.title: Avoid moving items before calculating its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` consumes the `Vec<String>` value. The following `items.len()` therefore borrows a moved value, producing Rust error E0382 and breaking all builds.

findings.title: Borrow items before inspecting them
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and consumes the `Vec<String>`. The subsequent `items.len()` therefore fails with a use-after-move compiler error.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` resolves differently from `latest`, `fromRevision` identifies the pinned revision but `changedPaths` are calculated from `latest`. Consumers replaying the changeset against `fromRevision` can receive an incompatible path set.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the declared base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to a revision other than "latest", changedPaths describes changes relative to latest while fromRevision remains the pinned revision. This violates the public Changeset contract that changedPaths is computed against, and replayed on, fromRevision.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When `pinnedTag` and `latest` resolve differently, `fromRevision` says consumers should replay from the pinned revision while `changedPaths` contains only changes since `latest`. Changes between the pinned revision and latest are omitted, so replaying this changeset produces an incomplete result.

findings.title: Update the query for the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any execution after upgrading will fail with an unknown-column error.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but src/query.sql:1 still executes `SELECT email FROM users`; databases upgraded through the migration will reject that query with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`. Any consumer running that query after migrations will fail with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing key
findings.whyItBreaks: A credential marked as live is now embedded in source, exposing it to every repository and PR reader and causing every deployment to use that same production billing identity.

findings.title: Restore the missing-key error contract
findings.whyItBreaks: makeClient is exported, but an unset BILLING_API_KEY no longer produces the previous explicit configuration error. Callers instead receive a client containing the hard-coded key, hiding missing deployment configuration.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credential loading
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line embeds a live billing API key in source and makes every deployment use it regardless of BILLING_API_KEY. Source readers can reuse the credential until it is revoked, and deployments can no longer independently rotate or scope their billing credentials.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: This source now contains a `bk_live_` credential. Anyone able to read the repository or its history can use it to authenticate against the production billing endpoint, and every deployment silently shares the same credential instead of using its environment-specific secret.

findings.title: Restore admin-only authorization for project purges
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed branches return "forbidden" for `isAdmin=true`, then allow any non-admin with an archived project to reach `db.delete(project.id)` and return "purged". This reverses the prior admin-only authorization.

findings.title: Require administrators before purging archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard returns "forbidden" for administrators, then allows deletion for any non-admin when `project.archived` is true. This reverses the prior authorization behavior and permits unauthorized permanent deletion.

findings.title: Allow administrators to purge archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: For an administrator and an archived project, this branch now returns "forbidden" before deletion. Previously that same valid combination deleted the project and returned "purged"; conversely, a non-admin can now purge an archived project.

findings.title: Preserve defaults when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when the path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The removed fallback previously converted that condition into default settings; startup now evaluates None["workers"] and raises TypeError, preventing startup.

findings.title: Restore the missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: `load_settings` returns `None` when `path` does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The changed line then subscripts `None`, raising `TypeError`; before this change, that same path returned the default `workers` value of 1.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-file fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (app/config.py:6). The removed fallback previously supplied workers=1; startup now evaluates settings["workers"] on None and raises TypeError instead of starting with defaults.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed branch logs a Gateway.Submit error and then returns nil, so the exported Charge function now reports failed charges as successful. The base revision returned the submission failure.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, this exported function logs it and then returns nil, making a failed charge indistinguishable from success to callers.

findings.title: Return gateway failures from Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, exported Charge logs the error then returns nil. A failed charge is therefore indistinguishable from a successful one, so callers can mark or persist failed payments as paid.

findings.title: Keep the tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Two tenants requesting the same setting name now share `settings:<name>`. After tenant A populates the cache, tenant B receives A's value without calling `store.fetch`, leaking or misapplying tenant-specific settings.

findings.title: Preserve invalidate's tenant-scoped public signature
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing JavaScript callers invoking `invalidate(tenantId, name)` now pass `tenantId` as the only consumed argument, so they delete `settings:<tenantId>` instead of the requested setting. TypeScript consumers also fail compilation after this exported API arity change.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed key at line 12 is based only on name, while the fetch remains tenant-scoped. Once tenant A caches a setting named "token", a request for the same name by tenant B returns the cached value at line 14 without calling store.fetch for tenant B, disclosing or applying tenant A's setting.

findings.title: Keep tenant identity in settings cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: `settingsFor("tenant-a", "theme", store)` caches its result under `settings:theme`; a later call for `tenant-b` with the same name returns that cached tenant-a value before calling the tenant-scoped `store.fetch`.

findings.title: Keep the existing Inventory construction path compatible
findings.whyItBreaks: Adding a required constructor parameter removes the class's prior zero-argument construction API. Existing TypeScript consumers using `new Inventory()` no longer compile; JavaScript consumers can still construct it but a positive-stock reservation dereferences the missing store.

findings.title: Do not change reserve from a synchronous boolean API
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `reserve` from `boolean` to `Promise<boolean>` breaks TypeScript consumers expecting a boolean. Existing JavaScript callers that branch directly on `inventory.reserve(sku)` receive a truthy Promise, so an out-of-stock reservation enters the success branch.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: The method reads `remaining` and then yields at `await this.store.save` before updating local stock. With stock 1, two concurrent calls can both observe 1, both save 0, and both return true, despite only one unit being available.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two callers can both read remaining=1 before either save resolves, then both save 0 and return true. This accepts two reservations for one item.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `await this.store.save(...)` occurs before `this.stock.set(...)`. Two concurrent calls with stock=1 can each read `remaining` as 1, both save 0, and both return true, confirming two reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: `retry` still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)` at src/jobs/retry.ts:12. After this change, the first retry waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) instead of 1,000 ms, and capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 hours).

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: `backoff(0)` now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but `retry` still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to its millisecond-based `sleep`. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) instead of 1 second.

findings.title: Remove the extra millisecond conversion in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return value is now milliseconds, but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000). Consequently, the first retry waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1,000 ms.

findings.title: Return file-close errors from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The new deferred f.Close() discards its error. If Flush succeeds but Close fails, Save returns nil and callers cannot distinguish the failed save from a successful one; the previous implementation returned the Close error.

findings.title: Propagate the close error after a successful flush
findings.whyItBreaks: The new deferred f.Close() discards its error, while Save now returns only w.Flush(). A delayed filesystem write error reported by Close therefore produces a nil result from this exported function; the base implementation returned that error.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The new deferred f.Close() call discards its error. Previously, after a successful Flush, Save returned f.Close()'s error; it now returns nil instead. Callers cannot detect a final close failure and may treat persistence as successful.

findings.title: Include each page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: The helper computes half-open [start, end) bounds, but range(start, end - 1) excludes end - 1. As a result, page_window(['a', 'b', 'c'], 0, 2) returns only ['a'], and render_page/summarize omit one row from each non-empty page.

findings.title: Include the page's last row
findings.whyItBreaks: The half-open bounds end is excluded by range(start, end - 1), so each non-empty page drops its last row; a one-row final page becomes empty. render_page and summarize consume this result directly, causing rows to disappear from output.

findings.title: Include the page endpoint in page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds are half-open [start, end), but `range(start, end - 1)` excludes `end - 1`. Every non-empty page loses its last row; with page_size=1, all pages render empty. `lib/pagination.py:45` passes this window directly to rendering.

findings.title: Return entries only while they are within the TTL
findings.whyItBreaks: Newly stored entries have an age below ttlMs, so this condition deletes them and returns null. Entries are returned only after expiry, reversing the cache contract.

findings.title: Filter completed jobs without splicing during forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item shifts later jobs left while forEach still advances its index. For `[done, done]`, the first removal shifts the second job to index 0 and it is skipped, so pruneDone returns a completed job. This also changes the previous non-mutating filter behavior by altering the caller's array.

findings.title: Return entries while they are still within the TTL
findings.whyItBreaks: A freshly stored entry has an age near zero, so `age > ttlMs` is false; `get` deletes it and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned.

findings.title: Remove all completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forward `forEach` iteration shifts the next element into the removed index, then `forEach` advances past it. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue. This also changes the prior API behavior by mutating the caller's array.

findings.title: Return cached values before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has an age below ttlMs, so this condition is false and get deletes it and returns null. Once an entry is expired, the condition becomes true and get returns stale data indefinitely.

findings.title: Filter completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forward forEach iteration shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the next index. For `[done, done]`, the first job is removed and the second remains, so pruneDone can return completed jobs.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before applying the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For players scored 8, 9, and 10 with n=2, rankScores returns [9, 8, 10], so the cutoff becomes 8; topPlayers then admits all players and slices input order, which can return 8 and 9 instead of the top two scores.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() compares numbers as strings. For scores [100, 20, 3], rankScores returns [3, 20, 100], making topPlayers(..., 1) use cutoff 3 and return the first input player rather than the player with score 100. formatBoard consequently displays an incorrect leader.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. With scores [2, 10, 11] and n=2, rankScores returns [2, 11, 10], making the cutoff 11; topPlayers then returns only the player scoring 11 instead of both 10 and 11.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` to compare an attacker-controlled signature with the expected HMAC can expose data-dependent timing, allowing a remote attacker to progressively infer a valid signature. `handle` uses this result to authorize processing of the webhook payload.

findings.title: Use a constant-time HMAC comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed equality comparison can stop at the first differing character, leaking prefix-match timing for the expected HMAC. `handle()` uses this result to authorize invoking the webhook processor, so restore a constant-time digest comparison.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` can stop comparison at the first mismatching character, making response timing depend on how much of the supplied signature matches the valid HMAC. `handle` exposes this result as 401 versus processing success for the attacker-controlled `given_signature`, allowing a timing oracle against webhook authentication.

findings.title: Keep balance changes inside the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after `_record_ledger`, committing the ledger entry before `_apply_balances` runs. An account update failure can therefore leave a committed ledger row and only a debit (or neither balance update), violating transfer atomicity.

findings.title: Keep both balance updates inside the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the `with db.transaction()` block exits, then the debit and credit execute outside that transaction. If either update fails, the function raises after recording a transfer; if the credit fails after the debit succeeds, balances are also left unbalanced.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction now commits after `_record_ledger` at line 23. If either balance UPDATE in `_apply_balances` then raises, the ledger row remains committed while one or both account balances were not updated; the base version rolled back all three writes together.

findings.title: Keep billing-day keys in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation derived the key from UTC. The changed local-time getters produce different keys for the same instant on hosts in different timezones; for example, 2026-08-10T00:30:00Z is 2026-08-09 in America/Los_Angeles. This shifts billing periods at UTC day boundaries.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving a billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return expression derives the date in the machine's local timezone rather than UTC. For example, `2026-01-01T00:30:00Z` produces `2025-12-31` on a UTC-08 host, so identical instants can be billed or grouped under different days by deployment timezone.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing-day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line uses host-local getters instead of the prior UTC getters. At 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z, a process in America/Los_Angeles returns 2025-12-31 rather than 2026-01-01, so billing classification varies by deployment timezone.

findings.title: Include tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level memo map is shared across all calls. After fetching account "a" for tenant "t1", a request for account "a" under tenant "t2" hits the same key and returns t1's Profile without calling fetchProfile, exposing stale or cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache is shared across all calls. After fetching profile `(tenantA, accountX)`, a later call for `(tenantB, accountX)` finds the same `accountX` key and returns tenantA's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile.

findings.title: Include tenant in the memo cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: Profiles are fetched with both tenant and account, but cached only by account. After readProfile("tenant-a", "acct-1", ...) caches a profile, readProfile("tenant-b", "acct-1", ...) returns tenant-a's cached Profile without calling fetchProfile, exposing cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `load` API now catches its own missing-key error and returns `""`, making failure indistinguishable from a stored empty value. `loadAll` at src/store.ts:12 maps this value into its result instead of propagating the missing-key failure.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed catch at lines 6-7 converts the explicitly thrown missing-key error into "". As an exported function, load no longer lets consumers distinguish absent data from a legitimately stored empty string; loadAll maps that behavior over every requested key.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch returns "" for a missing key, collapsing the exported function's error channel into a valid string value. loadAll maps through load at src/store.ts:12, so it now returns an array containing "" for missing keys rather than propagating the missing-key error.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config contract for retry
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers of retry that provide the formerly required { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check because timeout and retries are now required. Existing JavaScript callers receive config.timeout as undefined: Date.now() + undefined becomes NaN, so the timeout guard is always false and calls run despite a previously-expired timeout.

findings.title: Expose terminal failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: When every invocation throws, retryBackground catches each exception and then returns void after exhausting retries—the same observable result as a successful invocation. As an exported API, this forces callers to treat failure as success.

findings.title: Preserve the existing retry Config contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers of retry with the formerly valid { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } config no longer type-check because timeoutMs was removed and retries became required. Untyped existing consumers instead produce deadline=NaN, so the timeout guard is always false and the prior timeout limit is silently disabled.

findings.title: Expose exhaustion failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: After every attempt fails, retryBackground returns void exactly as it does after success. As an exported API, this forces callers to treat permanent failure as a successful no-result and can cause subsequent work to proceed after the requested operation never completed.

findings.title: Make retryBackground actually run in the background
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported name promises background/non-blocking execution, but the implementation synchronously invokes fn() before returning. A caller using this API to avoid blocking will instead block for the full callback duration.

findings.title: Expose exhaustion failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: After every attempt throws, the function returns void exactly as it does after success. Its public callers cannot distinguish an exhausted retry operation from a completed one and can treat failed work as successful.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now permits numeric values, but `value.length` is invalid for numbers. The changed component therefore fails TypeScript checking when compiled.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now accepts `number`, but the changed implementation reads `value.length`, which does not exist on numbers. This produces a TypeScript error and cannot correctly produce a length label for numeric values.

findings.title: Convert numeric values before measuring length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now accepts numbers, but number values have no length property. Typed builds report TS2339 here; if transpiled without type checking, `<Field value={123} />` renders `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Preserve sufficient buffer space for Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` at line 140 now inherits `spawnSync`'s 1 MiB default `maxBuffer`. A larger textual PR diff causes the synchronous child process to fail before a review bundle is produced, and `runGithub` posts a failed check instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Preserve the larger buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed wrapper materializes the full patch at src/adapters/github.ts:140. Removing its prior 64 MiB maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default, so a textual diff over 1 MiB fails while collecting the patch rather than being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore Git's 64 MiB stdout buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB when omitted. The adapter captures the full `git diff` output at src/adapters/github.ts:140, so a patch over 1 MiB causes the Git child process to fail and `git()` throws instead of publishing a review.

findings.title: Keep Codex invocations read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes the child Codex process use its configured sandbox policy. If that policy permits workspace writes or unrestricted access, model-requested commands can modify or delete `opts.repoPath`, which is passed as the process working directory.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed argument array removes the explicit `-s read-only` override. The Codex subprocess is run in `opts.repoPath` and receives the review prompt, so a write-capable ambient Codex sandbox configuration can allow a review to modify the repository.

findings.title: Restore the read-only sandbox for Codex runs
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed argument list invokes Codex with opts.repoPath as its working directory but no longer supplies the read-only sandbox. Prompts can therefore cause writes or deletions in the reviewed repository under Codex's default/configured sandbox.

findings.title: Generate the review bundle from the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed lines generate both `patch` and `changedFiles` from `baseSha` to `HEAD`, while this function still posts the review and check to `headSha` at src/adapters/github.ts:178-179. If the checkout is a PR merge commit, HEAD includes a synthetic merge result rather than the PR head, so the review can describe changes that do not belong to the commit receiving it.

findings.title: Diff the configured PR head rather than checkout HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the runner checkout HEAD (for example, a pull-request merge checkout), the bundle's headSha and review/check target remain PR_HEAD_SHA, but patch and changedFiles describe HEAD. The reviewer can analyze merge-checkout-only content or produce inline locations that do not match the commit receiving the review.

findings.title: Diff from the PR merge-base, not the base branch tip
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the current base-branch tip and the PR branch was created before newer base commits, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes base-only commits as reverse changes. Both the review patch and changed-file set can therefore contain files and hunks outside the PR.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed String.prototype.replace calls interpret $&, $`, $', and $$ in dynamic replacement strings. bundle.patch can contain these sequences from reviewed source, causing the critic prompt's patch evidence to be omitted or rewritten; serialized bundle and candidate payloads are affected similarly.

findings.title: Preserve dollar sequences when interpolating prompt data
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed direct replacement strings cause String.prototype.replace to interpret `$&`, `$`` , `$'`, and `$$` in bundle, patch, or candidate data. For example, a patch containing `$&` is replaced with the matched `{{PATCH}}` token before the critic receives it. The prior callback replacements inserted these values literally.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt payloads during replacement
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets $&, $`, $', and $$ in string replacement values. Patch, bundle, or candidate JSON containing these sequences is transformed before reaching the review or critic model, so the supplied context can be corrupted or include surrounding prompt text.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed commit in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: The review result is computed for `headSha`, but this fallback POST now omits `commit_id`. GitHub defaults an omitted commit ID to the PR's most recent commit. If the PR is updated after `headSha` is captured and the first POST fails, the fallback can publish a review against the newer, unreviewed commit while the check remains attached to the old SHA.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed fallback request omits `commit_id`. GitHub defaults an omitted value to the PR's most recent commit, so if the PR advances after `headSha` was captured and the primary review request fails, the review generated for the captured diff is posted against the newer commit.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the JSON request fails, this fallback omits `commit_id`. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, while this run computed its patch and verdict from `headSha`. If a commit is pushed while the review is running, the fallback can submit a passing or blocking review for code Needlefish never analyzed.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer now collapses invalid required fields into a valid-looking Finding: invalid severities become P1, invalid categories become bug, and missing locations become an empty file with line 0. Consumers of normalizeReview can therefore receive and act on malformed review output without any error signal.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-finding failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid finding fields now become a real-looking P1/bug finding with empty or zero-valued required fields. normalizeReview maps every finding through this conversion, so callers receive actionable-looking output rather than a validation failure.

findings.title: Keep normalizeReview's strict-mode API
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported strict parameter is source-breaking for TypeScript consumers calling normalizeReview(raw, false). JavaScript consumers can still pass false, but it is ignored and malformed findings are now returned as normalized defaults instead of being omitted.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed normalization converts invalid reviewer output into a valid-looking Finding: an unrecognized severity becomes P1, an invalid category becomes bug, and absent location fields become an empty file with line 0. normalizeReview immediately returns these fabricated findings to callers, which can incorrectly request changes or emit unusable annotations.

findings.title: Keep the repository explicit when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For `workflow_dispatch`, the event does not provide PR SHAs, so the changed commands at lines 38-39 run before the first checkout. With neither `-R` nor `GH_REPO`, `gh pr view` must discover a repository from a Git remote, which a fresh Actions workspace does not yet have. The dispatch workflow therefore fails before it can check out the requested PR.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository when resolving dispatch PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD and EVENT_BASE are empty, so the changed branch invokes gh pr view before any checkout. Without -R, gh must infer a repository from the workspace; on a fresh runner there is no checked-out repository context. Its failure is embedded in echo command substitution, producing empty head/base outputs, and the checkout at line 45 may then resolve the default or unintended ref rather than the requested PR.

findings.title: Keep the repository argument when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this step runs `gh pr view` before the checkout at .github/workflows/review.yml:42. The changed commands no longer provide a repository, and there is no checked-out git remote for gh to infer one from; manual dispatches therefore fail to resolve head/base SHAs.

findings.title: Continue rejecting malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or invalid required fields now become empty strings or arrays instead of throwing. A malformed model response is therefore indistinguishable from a legitimate review with zero findings, allowing callers to treat failed review generation as a clean result.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review errors
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported parser previously threw for a non-object or any missing required review field. It now returns an indistinguishable empty RawReview instead, so an invalid or truncated upstream response can be reported as a legitimate review with no findings or risks.

findings.title: Reject malformed review outputs
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or wrongly typed required fields now become empty strings/arrays instead of surfacing malformed model output. This exported normalizer makes callers conflate an invalid response with a legitimate clean review.

findings.title: Resolve requested PR refs for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch has no pull_request payload. The changed checkout falls back to github.ref, and PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA are empty, while the selected pr_number is only supplied to the CLI. A manually dispatched review therefore runs against the workflow branch rather than the requested PR revision and lacks its comparison SHAs.

findings.title: Resolve refs before manually reviewing a PR
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The changed checkout expression therefore uses github.ref—the branch selected when dispatching—instead of the requested pr_number's head. The changed PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA expressions are also empty, so the CLI cannot receive the requested PR's resolved SHAs.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR before checking it out
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The changed checkout falls back to github.ref and the base fetch falls back to main, neither of which is derived from the required pr_number input. A manual review can therefore inspect a non-PR checkout against the wrong base branch.

findings.title: Preserve the Git buffer limit for large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed spawnSync call no longer sets maxBuffer, so `git diff` uses Node's default 1 MiB output limit. `runLocal` passes that full diff to this helper at src/adapters/local.ts:100; diffs exceeding the limit cause the Git invocation to fail before a review is produced.

findings.title: Preserve the enlarged buffer for Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the entire patch through `git(["diff", ...])` at lines 98-100. Removing its 64 MiB `maxBuffer` restores `spawnSync`'s 1 MiB default, so a repository diff exceeding that size is terminated with a max-buffer error and the review aborts instead of producing a bundle.

findings.title: Restore sufficient buffer for Git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the entire patch through `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])` at line 100. Without an explicit `maxBuffer`, `spawnSync` uses Node's 1 MiB default; a larger legitimate PR exceeds that buffer and the wrapper throws before any review is performed. The prior implementation allowed 64 MiB.

findings.title: Scope the PR diff command to GITHUB_REPOSITORY
findings.whyItBreaks: `gh pr diff` is invoked without `--repo`, and `ghText` does not set a working directory. It therefore resolves the PR from the process working directory rather than the explicitly selected `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`; when those differ, the bundle can combine target-PR metadata with another repository's patch.

findings.title: Keep review execution errors as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path now passes `neutral` to `postCheck`, which posts that conclusion as a completed GitHub Check Run. An errored review is thus published as neutral instead of the previous failure, so it no longer reports a failing Needlefish check.

findings.title: Report review execution failures as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed catch path submits a completed GitHub check with conclusion "neutral" when review execution or result posting throws. The same path submitted "failure" before this diff, so an incomplete review is now represented as a non-failing check rather than a failed one.

findings.title: Keep review errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed catch path posts a completed `neutral` Needlefish check after a review error. A required GitHub check with a neutral conclusion is merge-satisfying, so repositories requiring this check can accept a PR whose review did not complete.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head is checked out at line 43, then line 59 executes its `src/cli.ts` while `GH_TOKEN` has pull-request and checks write permissions (lines 16-19, 56). A same-repository PR can modify that CLI to forge review/check results or use the token to alter PR state, defeating the review boundary previously provided by the trusted main checkout.

findings.title: Restore a checkout containing the review tool
findings.whyItBreaks: The checked-out PR head contains only `.github/workflows/review.yml` and `.needlefish/answers.json`; it has no package manifest, node_modules, or `src/cli.ts`. Consequently `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` cannot find a project manifest, so every review job fails before the review step.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed install and review commands run after checking out the same-repository PR head. A PR can therefore alter package install hooks or src/cli.ts and execute that code with GH_TOKEN plus pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions on the self-hosted runner, allowing it to forge review/check results or compromise the runner.

findings.title: Restore a trusted reviewer checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR head now supplies both dependencies and src/cli.ts. A same-repository PR can change those files to execute arbitrary code during review, with GH_TOKEN and pull-request/check write permissions on a self-hosted runner. The prior workflow deliberately isolated the untrusted target from the trusted tool checkout.

findings.title: Do not invoke a CLI absent from this repository
findings.whyItBreaks: At the reviewed head, the repository contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install --frozen-lockfile cannot install this project and the final command cannot resolve src/cli.ts, so every review job fails before producing a review.

findings.title: Retain the P1 fallback for invalid severities
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding now maps absent, malformed, or whitespace-padded severities to P3. normalizeReview emits that normalized value for every finding, so review output that previously retained a conservative P1 fallback is silently downgraded.

findings.title: Preserve severity canonicalization before validation
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview` maps untyped raw findings through `normalizeFinding`. Values previously canonicalized successfully, such as `" p1 "` or `"p0"`, now fail the exact membership check and are emitted as `P3`, hiding real high-severity findings.

findings.title: Normalize severity before validating it
findings.whyItBreaks: `normalizeReview` maps untyped JSON findings through this function. Values such as `"p0"` or `" P1 "`, which previously normalized to valid P0/P1 severities, now fail the exact match and are emitted as P3.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit `env` option causes `spawnSync` to inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The prompt is passed directly to `codex exec`, so the model and commands it invokes can read and potentially exfiltrate these credentials despite the read-only filesystem sandbox.

findings.title: Restore GitHub-token scrubbing for the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit `env` option makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The base revision explicitly removed these credentials before launching Codex; the subprocess now receives them.

findings.title: Restore GitHub-token scrubbing before launching Codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed spawnSync call omits its env option, so Node inherits process.env. GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN now reach the prompt-driven Codex child, removing the previous credential boundary.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard for self-hosted execution
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach this self-hosted job. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled head SHA, installs its dependency graph, and executes its `src/cli.ts`, giving a fork author arbitrary code execution in the self-hosted runner environment. GitHub may restrict the `GITHUB_TOKEN` for fork PRs, but that does not isolate the runner itself or any credentials, caches, network access, or persistent state it exposes.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job condition schedules this self-hosted workflow for fork PRs. It checks out the fork-controlled PR SHA and then runs `pnpm install` plus the checked-out CLI, allowing a fork author to execute arbitrary code in the self-hosted runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed condition at line 19 allows fork-origin pull_request events to run on the self-hosted runner. The job checks out the fork head at lines 22-25, installs its dependencies at line 29, and executes fork-controlled src/cli.ts at line 35.

findings.title: Keep zero-duration runner settings valid
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, an explicit NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 caused SIGKILL escalation immediately after SIGTERM. This change silently substitutes the 5000 ms fallback, so existing deployments configured for immediate escalation now wait five seconds. The same regression changes NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 from immediate completion after SIGKILL to a two-second wait.

findings.title: Keep zero as a valid runner duration
findings.whyItBreaks: `0` was previously accepted and schedules immediate timeout phases. The changed `> 0` guard instead applies the fallback: `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` becomes 5000ms, and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` becomes 2000ms.

findings.title: Preserve zero as an immediate runner timeout duration
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed validation rejects explicit `0` and returns the 5000 ms or 2000 ms fallback instead. Those values directly control the SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL grace period and the subsequent give-up timer, so callers can no longer request immediate escalation.

findings.title: Restore coverage for hotspots omitted by the mapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Selecting only MAX_HOTSPOTS removes every later mapped hotspot, and the deleted tail-coverage backstop no longer deep-reviews changed files absent from the selected set. Those files are not represented in the merged deep-review candidate.

findings.title: Keep reviewing when one deep-review call fails
findings.whyItBreaks: A throw from runCodex, extractJson, or normalizeReview at this line now rejects reviewLarge immediately. The removed per-hotspot handling previously retained completed work, continued later hotspots, and returned a blocking residual risk.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from successful deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep-review residual_risks are no longer accumulated; candidateMerged always serializes an empty array to the critic. A blocking uncertainty found by a deep pass can therefore be lost before the final verdict is derived.

findings.title: Deep-review every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews now process only the first six mapped hotspots. Any changed file omitted by the mapper or excluded by MAX_HOTSPOTS is never sent to deep review, so its findings can be absent from the final review.

findings.title: Keep deep-pass failures as blocked review results
findings.whyItBreaks: A failed or malformed deep response now rejects the exported review() call at this line. Previously the failure was converted into a blocking residual risk and the remaining hotspots still produced a report.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Deep-review residual_risks are discarded when candidateMerged is constructed. The critic at src/core/review.ts:118 therefore cannot receive a deep pass's blocking risk, and deriveVerdict at src/core/review.ts:122 can return a non-blocking verdict.

findings.title: Review changed files omitted by the selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews retain only six hotspots. After removing the tail-coverage hotspot, any changed file not named by those six is never sent to deep review and is not reported as unreviewed.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks returned by deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each successful deep review can return blocking residual risks, but this replacement supplies an empty array to the critic. The critic and final verdict can therefore return PASS despite a deep reviewer explicitly reporting unresolved, verdict-blocking evidence.

findings.title: Preserve review focus and depth for large patches
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed large-patch map payload omits bundle.focus and bundle.deep, so review requests that supply these inputs no longer pass their requested scope/depth to the map pass. Small-patch reviews still serialize the complete Bundle, making this a route-specific behavior regression.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, minutes is computed as 1 while the remainder rounds to 60, rendering "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". The prior implementation rounded total seconds before deriving minutes and seconds.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations such as 119500ms, minutes is computed as 1 while seconds rounds to 60, so review output reports `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations from 119500ms through 119999ms, `minutes` is 1 while the rounded remainder is 60, so rendered review stats show `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: For input "0", Number.isInteger(parsed) is true and parsed < 0 is false, so this exported parsePositiveInteger function returns 0 despite its error contract requiring a positive integer.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function promises and reports that values must be positive, but zero now passes validation and is returned. Callers can therefore receive an invalid zero value while trusting the parser's positive-integer contract.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed predicate accepts `0`, while the exported function and thrown error promise a positive integer. Consumers can now receive zero from this parser despite that contract.
